answer:
**One person's treatment can change another person's outcome.** A new feed changes which creators receive exposure, affecting content available to both groups. A pricing policy changes driver movement and shared supply, affecting riders assigned to control. Simple user-level comparisons can therefore mix direct effects with spillovers. [1](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

**The counterfactual is no longer isolated.** A control user in a heavily treated market may not experience the same environment they would under a full control rollout. The experiment can estimate a mixture-specific effect rather than the intended all-users deployment effect.

Graph-cluster randomization groups strongly connected users to reduce cross-group interaction. Geographic splits separate markets when geography contains much of the interference. Switchbacks alternate treatment over time for a shared system, with randomized schedules and appropriate washout/carryover handling.

Each design has costs: clusters reduce the number of independent units and may differ in size; geographies can differ systematically; time switches can be confounded by temporal patterns or persistent effects if designed poorly. There is no universal design that removes all interference.

Define the exposure mechanism and desired estimand before choosing the randomization unit. Analyze uncertainty at that unit, not by pretending every event is independent. Use domain knowledge about networks, movement, and carryover to make the experimental boundary approximate the actual interaction boundary.

**Technical details and references.**

Interference means one user's outcome depends on others' treatment assignments. A treated driver or feed user can change the environment experienced by control users, so an individual-level contrast may not estimate the all-treated versus all-control policy effect. [1](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

Graph clusters reduce cross-arm edges; geographic splits separate markets but provide fewer independent units; switchbacks alternate treatment over time in a market, requiring washout and control of temporal effects. Each trades bias, variance, and operational feasibility.

Define the exposure and estimand first. Analyze at the randomization unit, account for within-cluster dependence, and test carryover/spillover sensitivity. Increasing the number of logged events does not compensate for having very few independent markets. Cluster boundaries and time blocks must reflect how interference actually propagates.
